params.why: keeps every coefficient of the printed trinomial small, as in the book's 2x^2 + 22x + 20

solution: The highest common factor of the coefficients ${=k}$, ${=s * m}$ and ${=c}$ is ${=k}$, so take ${=k}$ out as a common factor first.
Divide each term by ${=k}$: ${=k}x^2{=sg}{=m}x+{=c} = {=k}(x^2{=sg}{=p + q}x+{=p * q})$.
Now factorise the trinomial $x^2{=sg}{=p + q}x+{=p * q}$. Look for two numbers whose product is ${=p * q}$ and whose sum is ${=s * (p + q)}$.
The numbers are ${=s * p}$ and ${=s * q}$, so $x^2{=sg}{=p + q}x+{=p * q} = (x{=sg}{=p})(x{=sg}{=q})$.
Put the common factor back in front: ${=k}x^2{=sg}{=m}x+{=c} = {=k}(x{=sg}{=p})(x{=sg}{=q})$.
notes: Entry point of the skill: the common factor k is an integer and the trinomial left inside the brackets is monic (x^2 + bx + c) with c > 0 and two DISTINCT roots of the same sign, so the signs are never a source of ambiguity and p + q != 0 (no difference of squares) and p != q (no perfect square, so the answer has one unambiguous factorised shape). Both the all-plus case (as in the book's 2x^2 + 22x + 20) and the all-minus case (x - p)(x - q) are generated from one skeleton. Constraint gcd(k, gcd(m, c)) == k asserts that k really is the highest common factor, because the inner trinomial is monic. The stem says 'completely' so a blind solver does not stop at (2x + 2)(x + 10). The parent q:g10m1s7-2-3:ex1-8-11 is printed as 2x^2 - 22x + 20 but its book solution works on 2x^2 + 22x + 20 (printing slip); this family is internally consistent in both signs. Trinomials with a leading coefficient other than 1 inside the brackets, mixed-sign roots, and the 2(2y^2 - 5y) - 24 re-bracketing twist are left to the standard and advanced tiers, which are not listed as gaps. No distractors (expression answer), so no misconception ids are used; the objective's catalogue is empty.
